issues.explanation: 'Dogs' as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of this military trauma profile: the other triggers/threat items center on interpersonal danger from men, being watched, and sudden human movements, with no supporting memory/appraisal content linking animals to the trauma. This makes the dog trigger clinically incoherent within the selected five components.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links Threat → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers, but the other selected strategies (overworking, never being alone with another person) plausibly manage interpersonal threat and hypervigilance, whereas gambling does not map clearly onto the endorsed trigger/threat pattern and reads as addressing a different problem domain.

vignette:
Priya Sharma is sixty-six years old, a midwife who has guided thousands of women through the most vulnerable moments of their lives, yet she cannot recall the last time she felt truly safe in her own body. The trauma happened during her brief service in the Army decades ago, when she was a young woman who believed in duty and structure. A superior officer, a man whose uniform gave him unquestioned authority, cornered her alone in a storage room after a long shift. She remembers the heavy click of the door, the way his rank insignia caught the fluorescent light, the flat certainty in his eyes as he watched her. She never reported it. What would have been the point? He was an officer, she was a nurse, and the uniform made him untouchable. She learned that night that men in authority could take what they wanted, that being watched meant danger was already upon you.

After leaving the service, Priya poured her considerable discipline into midwifery. The work felt like redemption, a world of women focused on life. But the sanctuary crumbled quickly. In the brightly lit corridors of the large teaching hospital where she works, the triggers press in from every side. She cannot be alone with a man. When a male anesthesiologist needs to review a patient's chart, she insists a female nurse join them in the consultation room, or she leaves the door wide open. She is certain that isolation with a male colleague is an invitation to harm. Authority figures—the Chief of Obstetrics, hospital security guards, anyone in a uniform—cause her stomach to drop. She has to fight the urge to walk away mid-conversation. She feels watched constantly: the security cameras in the hallways, the eyes of husbands and partners in the waiting room, a nurse glancing her way. She interprets these gazes as evaluative, predatory, a prelude to something terrible.

To manage the constant pressure of this threat, Priya has constructed a rigorous internal system. She throws herself into her work with an intensity that exhausts her colleagues. She takes back-to-back shifts, takes on the most difficult high-risk deliveries, stays late to write notes. Exhaustion is the only thing that quiets her mind. She makes sure never to be isolated. She eats lunch in the bustling cafeteria rather than the breakroom, and she always walks to the parking lot with someone else. She is perpetually vigilant for dangerous people, scanning the faces and postures of everyone around her. A man walking too close, a raised voice in triage, a sudden gesture from a patient's partner—her body shoots into full alarm before her mind can catch up. She is unable to relax, even at home. Her husband of forty years, Raj, will reach out to her on the couch, and she flinches. A sudden movement from him puts her immediately on guard. He has learned to announce himself before entering a room. The distance between them has grown into a chasm she does not know how to cross. He sees her exhaustion and her fear, but she has never told him the full story, and the silence has become a permanent feature of their marriage.

What finally drove her to seek help was a moment during a routine delivery. A young father stood up abruptly from his chair to see his laboring wife. The sudden movement was all it took. Priya's vision tunneled. The hospital room dissolved, and she was transported back to that supply room. She did not drop the baby, she did not flee the room, but for several seconds she was completely frozen, a terrified young nurse in an army uniform again instead of the seasoned midwife she had worked so hard to become. Afterwards, she locked herself in a supply closet and sobbed. She realized then that the strategies she had relied on for decades—the overwork, the isolation management, the constant scanning—were no longer containing the fear. They were hollowing her out. At sixty-six, with a career she loves and a marriage she is losing, Priya is here because she is terrified that if she does not find another way to live, she will spend the rest of her life waiting for the attack that already happened. She is desperately hoping that somewhere in the telling, she might finally find a way to let her guard down.
